citation: Wang CF, Gerner P, Schmidt B, Xu ZZ, Nau C, Wang SY, Ji RR, Wang GK. Use of bulleyaconitine A as an adjuvant for prolonged cutaneous analgesia in the rat. Anesth Analg 2008;107:1397-1405
text_quality: ok (9 PDF pages, complete including references; the extraction renders symbols as odd glyphs, e.g. the plus sign, the micro sign, plus-or-minus, less-than and equals; quotes copied character for character from texts/S-686-36.txt)
design: laboratory study in two parts: (1) whole-cell patch-clamp of HEK293t cells expressing human Nav1.7 and rat Nav1.8 sodium channels; (2) controlled animal experiment in rats - single injection into skin, blinded observer, cutaneous trunci muscle reflex (CTMR) to pinprick as the nociception outcome, with skin histology (haematoxylin and eosin, read by a pathologist) and PGP9.5 immunohistochemistry of skin, sections coded in a blinded fashion
population: HEK293t cells (transfected); male Sprague-Dawley rats, 250-300 g, Charles River; skin of the shaved dorsal thoracolumbar region, and hindpaw skin for part of the immunohistochemistry
n: rats: groups of six per injected test solution (CTMR); patch clamp n=5-7 per condition; PGP9.5 fibre counts: 9 sections from 3 animals per group (saline group and treated group); three rats in one high-concentration group
setting: Departments of Anesthesiology, Perioperative and Pain Medicine and of Pathology, Brigham and Women's Hospital, Harvard Medical School, Boston; animal protocol approved by the Harvard Medical Area Standing Committee on Animals
intervention: single injection of bulleyaconitine A (BLA) alone; BLA with lidocaine; BLA with epinephrine; BLA with lidocaine and epinephrine (a concentration series of BLA in the mixture). Drugs were freshly prepared in physiological saline
comparator: the lidocaine-with-epinephrine mixture alone (the control solution for the CTMR experiments); saline (the control group for the PGP9.5 fibre counts and the contralateral control side for pinprick). There was no plain-lidocaine-with-epinephrine arm and no plain-lidocaine arm in the histology or immunohistochemistry
route: subcutaneous injection into shaved dorsal thoracolumbar skin, raising a circular wheal that was marked with ink; for part of the PGP9.5 work a smaller injection into paw skin. The paper calls this a model of infiltration anaesthesia; it does not describe any injection as intradermal
duration: CTMR measured at intervals from injection to full recovery (up to about 144 h, i.e. about 6 days). Histology (haematoxylin and eosin): skin taken after full recovery, about 6 days after injection. PGP9.5 immunohistochemistry: skin taken about 24 h (one day) after injection. Single injection only - no repeated dosing
outcomes: peak sodium current block (resting, inactivated, use-dependent); CTMR as % maximum possible effect, duration of complete nociceptive blockade, time to full recovery, area under the %MPE-time curve; clinically observed systemic side effects and deaths; skin histology with an inflammation score; number of PGP9.5-immunostained nerve fibres per optical field in paw and back skin

key_results.quote: Drug solutions ([dose figure omitted]) were injected subcutaneously via rat shaved dorsal skin. Inhibition of the cutaneous trunci muscle reflex was evaluated by pinpricks. Skin cross-sections were stained with hematoxylin and eosin or with antibodies against PGP9.5.
Groups of six rats were injected with each test solution.
To determine whether nerve degeneration occurred after the drug injection, we performed immunohistochemistry in the hindpaw and back skin using a PGP-9.5 antibody that stained all nerve fibers.
The times of animal termination in these experiments are specified in the figure legends and all sections were coded in a blinded fashion.
In a control experiment, lidocaine ([dose figure omitted]) plus epinephrine ([dose figure omitted]) produced a short complete nociceptive blockade, approximately 1 h in duration.

Tissue toxicity after co-injection of BLA [dose figure omitted] along with [dose figure omitted] lidocaine and [dose figure omitted] epinephrine was examined in cross-sections of the rats’ skin tissue by a pathologist (Dr. Berigitta Schmidt). There were no apparent changes in histology compared with the control sections, except for mild lymphocytic perivascular infiltration approximately 6 days after co-injection.
Inflammation scores in and around the injected area, however, were not significantly different from the control.

Furthermore, we observed no apparent loss in PGP9.5 immunostained peripheral nerve fibers in both the back and paw skins approximately 1 day after co-injection (Fig. 7). The number of nerve fibers in each optical field for paw skins, for example, ranged 18 –24 (mean ⫾ se ⫽ 21.3 ⫾ 0.7, in 9 sections from 3 animals) in the saline group and 19 –23 (21.6 ⫾ 0.5, P ⫽ 0.732) in the BLA-treated group.
The epidermis layer of the skin is shown on top, followed by the dermis, muscle, and subcutaneous layer.
saline (left panel), control side; Bulleyaconitine A (BLA) (right panel), injected side.
Skin samples were taken approximately 24 h after injection. … Arrows indicate nerve fibers in the epidermis of the skin.

Even though cutaneous analgesia lasted for several days after co-injection of BLA/lidocaine/epinephrine, we observed no tissue damage in the cross-sections of the skin surrounding the injected site. The epidermis, dermis, and blood vessels all appeared intact.

Furthermore, the possibility that BLA exhibited selective toxicity towards peripheral nerve fibers was excluded by PGP 9.5 immunostaining. The number of peripheral nerve fibers remained unchanged one day after BLA injection.

author_limitations.quote: We used hNav1.7 because it was available to us as a gift from Dr. Klugbauer.
Four alternative explanations could be considered for this synergistic action.
Additional studies using various pain models will be needed to test these possibilities.
